examples.title: Carbon dioxide on Europa

orientation.note: A longitude-latitude map of the whole body. The first stored row is the north pole, the first column starts at 0 degrees east longitude and east runs to the right.

examples.note: The grey areas are longitudes and latitudes no cube saw, or saw too obliquely to measure.

examples.title: Europa at 12.8 microns

orientation.note: The stored rows of the resampled image, the first at the bottom. The frame is rotated on the sky: north is 70.6 degrees and east 340.6 degrees clockwise from up, measured from the image's own WCS.

examples.note: The four dithered exposures cover a cross-shaped area, and the grey corners were never on the detector. The grey hole in the middle of the disc is saturation: every contributing pixel there was rejected, so the level-3 combination gives those output pixels zero weight and no value.

examples.title: Europa's oxygen aurora

orientation.note: A grid fixed to the body, 0.0496 Europa radii a pixel, drawn as the stack writes it: body north up and celestial east left.

examples.note: Background scatter runs to about 30 R either side of zero, so the mid grey over most of the frame is noise, not emission.

examples.title: The 450 nm sodium chloride band on Europa

orientation.note: A longitude-latitude map of the whole body. The first stored row is the north pole, the first column starts at 0 degrees east longitude and east runs to the right.

examples.note: The four scans leave gaps; grey is where no scan reached or the surface was seen more than 60 degrees from face on.

examples.title: Europa in front of Jupiter

orientation.note: North up and east left, from the frame's own WCS.

examples.note: Jupiter's far-ultraviolet disc fills the frame and Europa is the dark spot on it. The grain is photon noise, about 20 counts a pixel over the 2,023 second exposure.

examples.title: Europa's thermal disc

orientation.note: North up and east left, from the image's own WCS.

product.definition: output/alma-europa/selfcal/Europa.selfcal.receipt.json (this stage has no pinned program file; the run states its parameters on the command line and records them in the receipt)

examples.note: The disc is 768 milliarcseconds across and the restoring beam 48 by 21 milliarcseconds, so the soft edge is the beam, not the limb.

examples.title: Ceres from the ground

orientation.note: The detector rows of the combined image, the first at the bottom. The reduced frame carries no world coordinates, so no sky direction is claimed.

examples.note: Ceres is resolved but small: about 52 pixels across at half its peak brightness, in the Ks filter through the S13 camera. The glow around it is the adaptive optics halo, which is blur in the data, not a rendering artefact, and the disc shows no surface detail at this scale.

examples.title: The X-ray halo around the Crab Nebula

orientation.note: Sky coordinates binned 9 by 9 pixels, 4.43 arcseconds a bin, the lowest row at the bottom. Sky x runs with falling right ascension and sky y with rising declination, so north is up and east is left.

examples.note: One dot is one detected X-ray photon, so this is counts, not brightness. The observation points 10.5 arcminutes north of the pulsar and the nebula itself is off the bottom of the array; what fills the lower chips is the halo around it. The dark lines are the gaps between the four ACIS-I chips.

examples.title: NGC 3132 in the near infrared

orientation.note: The stored rows of the re-made mosaic, the first at the bottom. The mosaic keeps the observation's own rotation: north is 303.4 degrees and east 213.4 degrees clockwise from up, measured from the mosaic's own WCS.

examples.note: At 3.6 microns most of what is bright is stars; the nebula's own shell is faint here.

examples.title: One JunoCam strip set of Europa

orientation.note: The three strips of frame 11 in the order the instrument reads them out: blue at the top, then green, then red. Nothing is rotated, and the strips are not combined.
